# **On the Accuracy of Effort Estimations based on COSMIC** **Functional Size Measurement: A Case Study**


[Ersin Ersoy](https://orcid.org/0000-0002-6100-9514) [∗]

Paycell
Turkey
ersin.ersoy@turkcell.com.tr

**Abstract**


[Selami Bagriyanik](https://orcid.org/0000-0002-5561-4283)
Singularity Software Technologies
Turkey
Bahcesehir University
Turkey
selamibagriyanik@gmail.com


[Hasan Sozer](https://orcid.org/0000-0002-2968-4763)

Ozyegin University
Turkey
hasan.sozer@ozyegin.edu.tr


Early effort estimation is both essential and challenging in software
development projects. Accurate effort estimation mainly relies on
accurate software sizing. COSMIC Function Point (CFP) is a means
for measuring the functional size of software. It is a standardized
method that can be applied to obtain size measurements based
on early artifacts such as the software architecture design. In this
paper, we present an industrial case study conducted to evaluate
the correlation between CFP measurements performed at the architecture design phase and the actual development efforts. The study
is performed in the context of a FinTech company that develops
a system comprising a backend, a native iOS application, and a
native Android application. We collect CFP calculations that are
performed at the architecture design phase of the corresponding
project. We also collect measurements regarding the actual effort
for 12 months. Then, we investigate the correlation between CFP
calculations and the measured effort. The actual effort can vary
for some development tasks that are associated with the same CFP
calculations. We analyze the relation of these variations with the
level of developer experience and the type of target platform. Our
results show that there is a significant correlation between size estimations made with CFP and the actual effort. The variance in effort
per CFP among varying types of platforms is statistically significant.
We also observe variance in effort per CFP among developers of
varying expertise levels.

**CCS Concepts**

- **Software and its engineering** → **Software creation and man-**
**agement** ; **Software development process management** ; **Soft-**
**ware development techniques** .

**Keywords**

COSMIC function point, software sizing, effort estimation, software
architecture, industrial case study

528


**Lay Abstract**

This paper discusses a study on estimating how much effort is required to build a software system. In particular, the study aims at
observing the link between effort estimations and size estimations.
The method called COSMIC Function Point (CFP) is used as a tool
for measuring the size of a software project from its initial design
stage. The research was applied on a financial mobile application
system in a fintech company. The researchers compared the estimated work, based on the CFP measurements taken at the design
stage, to the actual work it took to complete the project over 12
months. They found that the same CFP measurement could mean
different amounts of work, depending on factors like how experienced the developer is or what platform the software is being built
for. The study found a strong link between the size estimations
made using CFP and the actual amount of work needed.

**1** **Introduction**

Estimating the cost and effort for a software development project
is one of the biggest challenges in software engineering. It impacts
several critical decisions like budget allocation, size of the development team, and schedule. Despite standardization efforts [ 12, 16 ]
for benchmarking development productivity, the current practice
mainly favors subjective estimation approaches (e.g., story points)
based on experience and requirement analysis rather than quantification based on design artifacts [15, 17].
Accurate estimation of cost and effort requires accurate quantification of the size of software in an early stage of the development
life-cycle [ 2 ]. COSMIC Function Point (CFP) is a means for measuring the functional size of software [ 3 ]. It is a standardized method
that can be applied to obtain size measurements based on early artifacts such as the software architecture design. Despite its success
potential proven by research results, the adoption of CFP in the
software development industry is still limited [ 15 ]. Consequently,
there is a lack of industrial case studies reported in this domain
except a few [7, 13, 32].
In this paper, we present an industrial case study conducted for
analyzing the correlation between CFP measurements performed


ESEM ’24, October 24–25, 2024, Barcelona, Spain E. Ersoy et al.


at the architecture design phase and the actual development efforts.
Our goal is to evaluate the accuracy of effort estimations performed
based on architecture-based CFP measurements. The study is performed in the context of a FinTech company that develops a system
comprising a backend, a native iOS application, and a native Android application. We collect CFP calculations that are performed
at the architecture design phase of the corresponding system. We
also collect measurements regarding the actual effort for 12 months.
Then, we investigate the correlation between CFP calculations and
the measured effort using the Pearson Correlation Coefficient [ 25 ].
The actual effort can vary for some development tasks that are
associated with the same CFP calculations. We analyze the relation
of these variations with the level of developer experience categorized as *junior*, *senior*, and *expert* . We also analyze the impact of
the target platform, which requires software development with particular programming languages. The considered platforms include
the backend (Java), iOS (Objective C and Swift), and Android (Java
and Kotlin). We employed Kruskal-Wallis test [ 11, 21 ] to evaluate
statistical significance.
Our results show that there is a significant correlation between
size estimations made with CFP and the actual effort. The variance
in effort per CFP among varying types of platforms is statistically
significant. We also observe variance in effort per CFP among developers of varying expertise levels; however, statistical significance
cannot be inferred due to the lack of enough data samples for this
comparison.
The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. We provide
background information on COSMIC CFP in the following section.
We summarize related studies in Section 3. We introduce our indus
trial case study in Section 4. We present and discuss the results in
Section 5. Finally, we discuss future work and conclude the paper
in Section 6.

**2** **COSMIC Function Point**

COSMIC stands for Common Software Measurement International

Consortium, and COSMIC Function Point is recognized as a standard (ISO/IEC 19761: 2011) for measuring the functional size of software [ 3 ]. CFP can be calculated early in the software development
life-cycle based on the software’s requirements and architecture
design, without needing to consider the implementation details.
It has been used for sizing software development projects [ 29 ] by
various companies [9, 14, 26, 27].
As an example consider the system architecture in Figure 1 and
a user scenario where *“the user wants to see all payment methods*
*that active in the system."* . The first step in the execution of this
scenario involves the movement of a data group containing user
intention (i.e., listing payment methods) from the user to the native
mobile application (iOS App or Android App) interface. This is
an Entry (E) data movement. The user information is sent to the
backend layer (Backend) in the second step. Since a boundary is
assumed between the mobile applications and the backend layer,
this transfer is considered as an Exit (X) data movement for the
mobile application and an Entry (E) data movement for the backend
layer. Setting a boundary is crucial for measurement coherence in
multi-layer or multi-tier architectures. Boundary configurations for
several application architectures are documented in Measurement

529


Strategy Patterns Guideline [ 28 ]. These architectural measurement
patterns ensure that CFP functional size measurements may be
compared. The third step collects information from the database
regarding the payment methods and saves the request for logging
purposes. These two activities are categorized as a Read (R), and a
Write (W) data movements, respectively. Next, the collected data is
sent to the applications (X data movement for the backend layer
and E data movement for mobile applications). Finally, payment
methods are listed on the mobile application (X data movement).
Note that there are two different native mobile applications and
hence they must be measured separately. Additionally, E and X
data movements for the backend layer are counted just once since
the same service is reused for both iOS and Android mobile applications. The total size is the sum of iOS App data movements,
Android App data movements and Backend (including Database)
data movements as 4 CFP + 4 CFP + 4 CFP = 12 CFP. In the follow
ing, we summarize related studies, in particular those that apply
software sizing and effort estimation based on CFP measurements
at the software architecture design phase.

**Figure 1: A high level architectural view of the object system.**


The first group of studies discussed above includes an architectural level analysis, while the second group does not relate measurements to the architectural design, basic architectural components,
and essential boundary assumptions that are necessary for CFP
measurement in case studies. Consequently, the consistency of the
project data used in the studies is difficult, if not impossible, to
verify. Hence, it is not possible to utilize these as a benchmark.
In this study, we focus on CFP measurements based on architectural components and boundary configurations that are explicitly
defined. We present an industrial case study as explained in the
following.

**4** **Industrial Case Study**

We conducted an industrial case study in the context of a Fintech [ 24 ] company, specifically Paycell [1] (a company of the Turkcell [2] group). In this case study, development tasks of the Paycell
mobile application, which has been downloaded more than twenty
million times, are measured by CFP and actual effort for 12 months.
The usage of the CFP method in this company is well established. It
has been used for effort estimation and software procurement since
2015. It has also been used as a velocity and value metric within
some agile teams in the company.
Figure 1 shows an architectural view of the object software
system. The client layer comprises two separate mobile applications,
each tailored for the iOS and Android platforms, respectively. The
iOS application was developed using Objective C and Swift, in
contrast, the Android application was constructed employing Kotlin
and Java. Also, there is a Java based backend application which

1 https://paycell.com.tr/
2 https://turkcell.com.tr/

530


serves as middle layer between client layers and other systems.
Other components include databases and domain services.

**4.1** **Research Questions**

The first goal of our study is to investigate if there is any correlation
between size estimations made with CFP and the actual effort. That
is, we would like to know if CFP can be a reliable proxy measure or
input for effort estimation. The second concern is about the affect
of developer expertise on development effort. Since CFP is a sizing
measure, the effort to implement features with the same CFP can
differ based on expertise. We would like to know to what extent
it does so. The final concern is related to the affect of the type of
platforms on development effort. We would like to know if the effort
for implementing features with the same CFP for various platforms
such as iOS, Android and backend differ, and if so, to what extent it
does. We formulate our research questions in alignment with these
concerns as follows:

  - **RQ1:** Is CFP a reliable proxy measure for effort estimation?

  - **RQ2:** How is the effort affected by the level of developer
experience?

  - **RQ3:** How does the effort differ for various platforms?

**4.2** **Data Collection**

We compiled a dataset from the Jira tool [ 1 ] that was being used
for tracking tasks in the project. The dataset includes 330 tasks that
were developed during 12 months. Table 3 lists a sample snippet
from the dataset. The first two columns list the Jira ID and the
(enumerated) name of the task. The other information collected
per task is collected in 4 columns, which are repeated for each
platform, Backend, Android, and iOS. The first two of these columns

**4.3** **Evaluation Methods and Metrics**

We measured the correlation between CFP measurements and ac
tual effort measurements to answer the first research question. The
correlation between two variables quantifies the strength and direction of their relationship. In statistics, the Pearson Correlation is a
commonly used measure of this relationship, and it has previously
been utilized in effort estimation studies [ 5 ]. In particular, we employed Pearson Product-Moment Correlation Coefficient (Pearson’s
r) [ 25 ] by the formula given in Equation 1 and then the statistical
significance is evaluated with an online p-value calculator [3] .

*𝑟* = � *𝑛* *𝑖* = 1 [(] *[𝑥]* *[𝑖]* [−] *[𝑥]* [¯][)(] *[𝑦]* *[𝑖]* [−] *[𝑦]* [¯][)] (1)

*𝑛* *𝑛*
~~√~~ ︃� *𝑖* =1 [(] *[𝑥]* *[𝑖]* [−] *[𝑥]* [¯][)] [2] ~~√~~ ︃� *𝑖* =1 [(] *[𝑦]* *[𝑖]* [−] *[𝑦]* [¯][)] [2]

The *𝑟* value represents the correlation coefficient, which ranges
from -1 to 1. An *𝑟* value of -1 indicates a perfect negative correlation between the two variables, while an *𝑟* value of 1 indicates a
perfect positive correlation. An *𝑟* value of zero indicates no linear
relationship between the two variables. Generally, it is accepted
that *𝑟* values between 0.5 and 1.0 indicate a strong correlation [8].
To address the second research question, we grouped the involved subjects based on their seniority levels for each platform
and calculated effort per unit CFP (measured in hours) for each
group and for each platform. We also grouped effort measurements
for tasks with the same CFP to test the statistical significance of
differences among these measurements for the three groups of
seniority levels.
Finally, we analyzed the variance in effort per unit CFP in hours
to answer the last research question. We calculated average effort
per CFP for each platform and compared these calculations. We
also tested the statistical significance of differences among measurements performed for the three platforms. We applied Kruskal-Wallis
test [ 11, 21 ] for testing statistical significance to answer the last
two questions. The Kruskal-Wallis test is a non-parametric statistical method used to compare three or more independent groups to
determine if there are statistically significant differences between
them. It is particularly useful when the assumptions for a one-way
analysis of variance are not met. As a non-parametric test, it does
not require the data to be normally distributed.

**5** **Results and Discussion**

We present and discuss the results in this section. Each of the
following three subsections focuses on a research question. We
conclude the section with a discussion of threats to validity.

**5.1** **RQ1 – Using CFP for effort estimation**

We calculated Pearson’s r and checked their significance with .05
significance level for each of the three platforms, Backend, Android
and iOS. The results are listed in Table 2. The sample size is listed
for each platform in the second column. The third column lists the
Pearson’s *𝑟* values, which are calculated as .82, .76, and .75, for the
Backend, Android, and iOS platforms, respectively. We see in the

We conclude based on these results that CFP sizing and calculated

**5.2** **RQ2 – Impact of experience on effort**

The second group of results are related to the seniority level of
developers as a potential factor that impacts the development efforts. We calculated hourly cost per unit CFP in the whole dataset
based on seniority level for each of the three platforms separately.
Results are depicted in Figures 2, 3, and 4, for Backend, Android
and iOS platforms, respectively. We can see in these charts that unit
cost decreases for all platforms when seniority level increases. The
amount of differences in effort for the three seniority levels varies
among the three platforms as discussed in the following.
We see in Figure 2 that the efforts per unit CFP for the Backend platform are calculated as 3.56 hours, 3.48 hours, and 2.16
hours for junior, senior and expert seniority levels, respectively.
The difference in average effort is not high between junior and
senior developers but we observe a significant reduction for expert
developers. The main reason for this result would be that the development activities are generally simple and similar to each other on
the Backend side. These activities mainly aim at forming a bridge
between native platforms and external services. Therefore, expert
developers can complete their tasks faster by using their dexterity.
We see in Figure 3 that the efforts per unit CFP for the Android
platform are 5.14 hours, 4.28 hours, and 3.91 hours for junior, senior
and expert seniority, respectively. This time, the difference of effort

532


**Figure 4: Effort per unit CFP in hours for the iOS platform.**

between senior and expert developers is less than the difference
between the junior and senior developers. We see a similar result
for the iOS platform, where the difference in effort between junior
and senior developers is much larger than the difference between
senior and expert developers. Figure 4 lists the efforts per unit CFP
for the iOS platform are 6.85 hours, 4.35 hours, and 4.01 hours for
junior, senior and expert seniority, respectively. We also intended
to apply a non-parametric test, namely Kruskal-Wallis test [ 11, 21 ]
to test the statistical significance of differences in effort for varying
seniority levels of developers. However, the size of our data samples
turned out to be insufficient ro infer statistical significance. As a
result, regarding *RQ2*, we conclude that significant effort differences
are observed among developers with varying seniority levels in our
case; however, statistical significance of these differences cannot be
tested due to the lack of enough data samples for this comparison.

**5.3** **RQ3 – Impact of platform on effort**

Figure 5 depicts a bar chart for effort per unit CFP, calculated as
3.43 hours, 4.47 hours and 4.34 hours for the Backend, Android
and iOS platforms, respectively. We observe that efforts differ for
each platform. Although the amount of difference is not high between the Android and iOS platforms, the measured effort is significantly lower for the Backend in comparison with the other two


ESEM ’24, October 24–25, 2024, Barcelona, Spain E. Ersoy et al.

**6** **Conclusion and Future Work**


**Figure 5: Effort per unit CFP in hours of each platform.**

platforms. We also applied a non-parametric test, namely KruskalWallis test [ 11, 21 ], which can be used even if the data are not normally distributed. The p-value turned out to be 6 *.* 5 × 10 [−][3], which
is much lower than the critical value, 0 *.* 05. This shows that the
difference is statistically significant as well.

**5.4** **Threats to Validity**

Our study is subject to validity threats and limitations. One of these
threats is related to the external validity [ 31 ] since the study is
conducted in the context of a single organization and it focuses
on a specific software system. The study can be conducted across
different application domains and organizations to increase the
generalizability of our results. However, this poses a significant
challenge due to the lengthy and intensive data collection process
it would require, along with the sustained support needed from
the organization. Despite the 12 months period considered for this
study, the data samples collected were not sufficient to test statistical significance for one of the research questions. Another threat
to our study is related to internal validity [ 31 ] concerning our CFP
measurements. Triangulation [ 22 ] was employed to mitigate this
threat, where multiple data sources are utilized for validation. Measurements were validated by two independent sources: the team
members and an independent department within the organization.
Finally, the categorization of subjects presents a potential threat to
the validity of this study. The seniority levels of developers (junior,
senior, expert) were determined based on the team’s self-assessment
of their expertise, and we have adopted their definitions directly.
In this study, we did not explicitly addressed Non-functional
Requirements (NFR) and their impact on effort estimations. There
are two primary considerations regarding NFR. First, NFRs (such
as security requirements) may initially appear difficult to measure
using CFP. However, this perception often changes with more indepth analysis, where a set of derived user stories actually map to
functional requirements to satisfy a particular NFR, each of which
can be measured using CFP. Second, while some other requirements
(e.g., satisfying a comment/code ratio) cannot be measured by CFP
but they typically affect the unit cost. As a result, NFRs are indeed a
significant factor that contributes to increased development effort;
however they are sometimes indirectly reflected to the development

costs.

533


We presented an industrial case study to evaluate the accuracy of effort estimations at the architecture design phase based on COSMIC
Functional Points (CFP) size measurements. The study is performed
in the context of a FinTech company that develops a system comprising a backend, a native iOS application, and a native Android
application. We collected CFP calculations that are performed at
the architecture design phase. We also collected measurements
regarding the actual effort for 12 months. Our results show that
there is a significant correlation between size estimations made
with CFP and the actual effort. The development effort can vary for
some tasks that are associated with the same CFP calculations. We

analyzed the relation of these variations with the level of developer
experience and the type of target platform. We observed significant
effort differences among developers with varying seniority levels
in our case; however, statistical significance of these differences
could not be tested due to the lack of enough data samples. We also
observed significant differnces in effort per CFP among varying
types of platforms and these differences turned out to be statistically
significant as well.
For future research, it would be beneficial to conduct analogous
case studies, incorporating a diverse range of teams and systems
from different application domains to improve the generalizability
of the results. Tool support can be utilized for (semi-)automated
CFP calculations based on standard and/or customized architectural
views. Previously, there have been attempts [ 20 ] to create domainspecific UML profiles for this purpose. Tools can be integrated
with development environments to estimate and track the effort
throughout the software development life-cycle.
